first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are directly addressed by the onboarding/signup path, and two independent inherited records (memory_86, memory_31) point the same way, which makes this the best-supported single-slot bet for durable qualified revenue rather than a one-quarter bump. I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing even though memory_73 maps most cleanly onto the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is the most expansive claim in the inherited set (acquisition lift, revenue lift, faster time-to-value, holding across both billing plans), and consolidated summaries tend to accumulate scope they did not originally have. Discount-led acquisition is also the direction whose apparent win most easily masks long-term damage — margin erosion, reference-price reset, and a cohort selected for price sensitivity that churns. So I am spending one verification pull on memory_73 specifically to see whether the original record supports that breadth, and one on memory_86 because it is the primary support for what I actually intend to do; if the archived record turns out to be a narrow self-serve test rather than a general onboarding finding, I should know that before committing the slot. Downstream value risk: cutting signup fields can degrade lead qualification data, which memory_44 suggests is what feeds the sales-assisted enterprise path — a self-serve activation gain that quietly starves enterprise pipeline quality would be a net loss against the stated objective, so the experiment must instrument enterprise pipeline quality and downstream conversion, not just week-one activation. All inherited findings are from days 12-61 under a pre-competitor market; the current environment may have changed their validity, so I want a real holdout and a decision horizon long enough to see retention, not just completion rates. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout for exactly that reason.
